strengths: Strong theoretical foundation: the paper rigorously proves in a simplified linear setting why post-training selection (PTS) and all-subspace learning (ASL) provably fail to recover Pareto-optimal submodels, while nested subspace learning (NSL) succeeds (Thms 4.1-4.3), with clean proofs building on Eckart-Young-Mirsky and careful measure-theoretic arguments.

The theoretical claims are validated empirically at multiple levels: controlled synthetic experiments matching the theory exactly (Fig 2), and a small-scale exhaustive search over all 10,000 possible submodels on MNIST (Fig 3) showing FlexRank recovers the true Pareto front despite weight sharing constraints -- a compelling sanity check bridging theory and practice.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning NLP (GPT-2, Llama 1B/3B/8B) and CV (DINOv3 from 300M to 7B parameters), with consistent and substantial improvements over SVD, DataSVD, and the SOTA ACIP baseline.

Insightful analysis of why ACIP's adapter training underperforms (interference among competing submodels, connecting back to the ASL failure mode), which strengthens the practical relevance of the theoretical framework.

Useful ablations isolating individual contributions: importance of joint/nested submodel training vs. independent training (Fig 8), limits of calibration sample size for SVD init (Fig 7a), and the necessity of end-to-end (vs per-layer) distillation (Fig 7b).
Demonstrates practical downstream usability by fine-tuning LoRA adapters on FlexRank submodels for math/code tasks.
Clear writing, informative figures, and a well-organized related-work comparison table (Tab 2) situating the method against prior low-rank compression approaches.
weaknesses: The theory is developed only for single-layer linear models; while helpful for intuition, its applicability to deep nonlinear transformer stacks (where FlexRank is actually deployed) relies entirely on empirical validation, and the paper itself notes (Fig 7b) that inter-layer nonlinear dynamics create additional gaps not captured by the linear theory.

No comparison against the most directly relevant elastic/flexible model baselines (FlexTron, LLaMaFlex) is performed, since these are only discussed qualitatively in the appendix and excluded from experiments due to lack of public code -- leaving open how FlexRank compares to the broader elastic-model literature beyond SVD-based methods.

The DP-based rank allocation assumes additive approximation errors across layers, a strong simplifying assumption acknowledged by the authors but not directly stress-tested for larger/deeper models beyond the overall downstream accuracy curves.

Reported post-adaptation results (Table 1) show steep degradation at smaller budgets (e.g., code accuracy dropping from ~18-37% to ~1-2% at 0.4x), which appears at odds with the paper's central claim of "graceful" degradation, and is not discussed or reconciled in the text.

Training was restricted to a limited regime (10k steps, roughly half an epoch on FineWebEdu) due to compute constraints; while honestly disclosed, this leaves open whether relative rankings among methods (e.g., vs ACIP) would hold under fuller training.

Efficiency/inference-speed claims in Sec 3.5 are purely theoretical (FLOP counting); no wall-clock latency or throughput measurements are provided to substantiate the deployment benefits central to the paper's motivation.

Main results figures (Figs 4, 5) lack error bars or variance estimates, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of gaps between FlexRank and baselines, particularly in mid-budget regimes where curves are close.
The Impact Statement is minimal and generic, providing no substantive discussion of potential risks or considerations specific to model compression/elastic deployment.

strengths: The paper provides a clean theoretical framework (Sec. 4) formalizing why post-training selection (PTS) and all-subspace learning (ASL) fail to recover Pareto-optimal nested submodels, and proves that nested subspace learning (NSL) does recover them in the linear-model case. The proofs appear rigorous and the linear-algebra arguments (Eckart-Young-Mirsky, balanced factorization penalty, measure-zero arguments) are carefully worked out.

The overall pipeline (per-layer data-aware SVD initialization, dynamic-programming-based global rank allocation assuming additive layer errors, and distillation-based joint refinement of nested submodels) is a sensible and reasonably novel combination of existing ideas (data-aware SVD, nestedness constraints, knowledge distillation) targeted at a real practical problem (elastic/adaptive deployment).
Empirical validation on a small MNIST-scale network (Sec. 3.4) that exhaustively compares to the true combinatorial Pareto front is a nice sanity check supporting the method's central approximation.

Experiments span multiple modalities and scales (GPT-2, Llama 3.2/3.1 up to 8B, DINOv3 ViT up to 7B), and show consistently more graceful degradation than SVD/DataSVD/ACIP baselines across these settings.

The paper includes informative ablations (sample size for DataSVD, need for end-to-end vs. per-layer-only training, importance of joint nested training vs. independently trained submodels) that help build an evidentiary case for design choices.
weaknesses: The comparison set is thin and somewhat dated/narrow for a method claiming SOTA: only naive SVD, DataSVD, and ACIP are compared against quantitatively; other closely related methods explicitly discussed in Table 2 (FWSVD, DRONE, ASVD, SVD-LLM, SVD-LLM V2, A3) are entirely absent from the empirical evaluation, and FlexTron/LLamaFlex are excluded with a justification (no released code/proprietary data) that, while understandable, still leaves the significance claim relative to the actual elastic-model competitive landscape largely untested.

Absolute performance numbers are weak: e.g., Table 1 shows post-adaptation accuracy on math/code dropping drastically even at 0.8x and 0.6x budgets (e.g., Code accuracy for Llama-3.2-1B falls from 18.63 at 1x to 9.30 at 0.8x and 3.34 at 0.6x), undermining the 'graceful degradation' narrative touted in the abstract/title for practically useful compression ranges.

Training cost is very high (2–8 A100 nodes for 2–6 days per model) for what is ostensibly a lightweight, distillation-based elastic model construction; the paper's own 'train-once, deploy-everywhere' framing is undercut by the fact that this upfront investment is substantial and the results are reported only under an admittedly limited-compute regime (Sec. D.4), making it hard to assess whether gains are an artifact of insufficient baseline training rather than a genuine algorithmic advantage.

The theoretical results in Sec. 4 are derived for a strictly linear, single-layer, noise-free setting with a fixed matrix M*, and extending this to deep nonlinear transformers (with attention, nonlinearities, and residual/cross-layer interactions) is a substantial leap that is not theoretically justified—only empirically gestured at via the ablation in Fig. 7(b)/Sec 5.3. The 'additivity of errors across layers' assumption underlying the core DP algorithm is acknowledged as 'strong' but never empirically validated beyond indirect ablations.

The claim that FlexRank 'recovers the true Pareto front' (Sec 3.4, Fig 3) is only demonstrated on a toy 4-layer MNIST model with K=10 ranks; generalizing this as a central empirical validation for billion-parameter LLMs/ViTs is a significant overreach given the scale gap.

Error bars/statistical significance are inconsistent: Table 1 reports ± values (presumably standard error across benchmarks) but the main Figures 4/5 show single curves with no variance/error bars, and it's unclear how many seeds or runs underlie the reported numbers, especially for the large models where training runs are prohibitively expensive (likely single-run results).

The DINOv3/ImageNet1K results claim 'performance comparable to full model' down to 30% of parameters, but the paper itself notes this may be an artifact of ImageNet1K being a much smaller/easier dataset relative to the pretraining distribution rather than reflecting a general property of the method, weakening the generalizability of this specific headline result.

The Impact Statement is essentially a boilerplate non-statement ('none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted here'), providing no genuine consideration of dual-use or downstream deployment risks despite the paper explicitly targeting broad deployment scenarios (edge devices, heterogeneous hardware).

Minor presentation issues: notation is dense and sometimes inconsistently used (e.g., overloading mk/Sr, budget notation beta vs rank r), and some figures (e.g., Fig. 6 and 7) lack sufficient captions/axis explanation to be self-contained without consulting the main text extensively.

strengths: Strong theoretical contribution: the paper rigorously analyzes three training strategies for rank-elastic models (PTS, ASL, NSL) in the linear model setting, proving that only nested training (NSL) provably recovers the Pareto front, while post-training selection and joint all-subspace training provably fail (Thms 4.1-4.3, with full proofs in the appendix). This gives a principled justification for the design of FlexRank beyond heuristic motivation.
The theory is directly validated with controlled synthetic experiments (Fig. 2) that visually confirm the predicted failure modes of PTS and ASL and the success of NSL.

A small-scale exhaustive-search experiment (Fig. 3, MNIST 4-layer network with 10,000 possible submodels) empirically shows that FlexRank recovers the true Pareto front obtainable only by brute-force independent training, which is a convincing sanity check that is rarely attempted in this literature.

Broad empirical evaluation spanning NLP (GPT-2, Llama-3.2-1B/3B, Llama-3.1-8B) and vision (DINOv3 from 300M to 7B parameters), showing consistent qualitative trends (graceful accuracy decay) across both modalities and a wide range of scales.

Useful and comprehensive ablations: effect of calibration sample size on DataSVD, necessity of end-to-end (vs per-layer) submodel training, and necessity of joint/nested submodel sampling vs single-budget training, which together support the paper's mechanistic story.

Clear positioning relative to prior low-rank compression methods (Table 2) and a thoughtful discussion of orthogonal architectural-elasticity methods (FlexTron, LLaMAFlex) in the appendix, with honest justification for why they are not directly compared against.

Practical efficient-inference trick (alternative basis via invertible G) that reduces FLOPs further without aggressive rank reduction, showing attention to deployability, not just the training recipe.
Reasonably transparent limitations and compute-accounting section (Sec. D.4), acknowledging that results are reported under constrained training budgets and could likely improve further.
weaknesses: The core theoretical guarantees (Thms 4.1-4.3) are proven only for single linear-layer factorization; their relevance to deep, nonlinear, multi-layer Transformer architectures is argued informally (via the additivity-of-errors assumption and the DP-based global ordering) but not theoretically extended, leaving a gap between the clean theory and the practical algorithm.

The claim of 'graceful degradation' is not fully supported by Table 1: post-adaptation (LoRA) results show severe drops at smaller budgets (e.g., code accuracy falling from ~18.6 to ~1.2 at 0.4x for Llama-3.2-1B), which seems to contradict the headline narrative and is not discussed or analyzed in the text.

Main results (Figs. 4, 5) are reported without error bars or variance estimates across seeds/runs, making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of the comparisons against SVD, DataSVD, and ACIP baselines.

Experiments are explicitly run under compute-limited regimes (10k steps, as discussed in Sec. D.4), and the paper acknowledges that both FlexRank and possibly the baselines (e.g., ACIP) might behave differently under larger compute budgets, which weakens the strength of the head-to-head comparisons.

No direct empirical comparison to the most relevant 'flexible/elastic network' baselines (FlexTron, LLaMAFlex), even though they are discussed qualitatively in the appendix; while the stated reasons (no public code, proprietary training data) are understandable, this leaves an important class of competing methods unevaluated.

The dynamic-programming search relies on a strong additive-error-across-layers assumption, whose quality is only indirectly validated (via the small-scale MNIST Pareto-front recovery experiment); no large-scale ablation quantifies how much this approximation costs relative to a non-additive or more exact search.

Wall-clock latency/throughput benchmarks are absent; the efficiency claims rest solely on theoretical FLOP counts (Sec. 3.5), which may not translate directly into real inference speedups on modern hardware/kernels.
The Impact Statement is essentially boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with potential risks or deployment considerations of elastic/compressed foundation models.

strengths: Strong theoretical grounding: the paper proves (in a tractable linear setting) why post-training selection (PTS) and all-subspace learning (ASL) fail to recover Pareto-optimal submodels, and why nested subspace learning (NSL) provably does. This gives a principled justification for the design choice (nested training) rather than relying on intuition alone.

The central theoretical claim is empirically validated in a controlled, exhaustively-searchable setting (Fig. 2, Fig. 3), showing FLEXRANK recovers the true Pareto front that would require training all 10,000 submodels independently.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning both NLP (GPT-2, Llama-3.2-1B/3B, Llama-3.1-8B) and vision (DINOv3 ViT-L to ViT-7B) with consistent gains over strong low-rank baselines (SVD, DataSVD, ACIP) across a wide range of budgets.

GAR (Gauge-Aligned Reparametrization) is a useful, broadly applicable practical contribution that closes much of the gap between naive low-rank factorization and dense compute, with empirical validation of the theoretical FLOP savings (App. D.4, Fig. 10).

Thorough ablations isolate the contribution of each component: SVD initialization sample-size sensitivity, the necessity of end-to-end submodel training vs. per-layer training, and the importance of joint/nested submodel sampling vs. training a single budget.

The additive-error assumption underlying the DP rank-selection procedure, while acknowledged as a simplification, is explicitly stress-tested in App. C.3 with quantitative metrics (Spearman correlation, violation rate, DP exact-match rate, regret), lending credibility to a key approximation.

Good positioning against related work, including a detailed comparison table (Tab. 2) and honest discussion of a concurrent work, as well as non-rank-based baselines (LLM-Pruner, LayerSkip) for broader context.
Post-adaptation experiments (LoRA finetuning of submodels on math/code) demonstrate practical downstream usability of the extracted submodels, not just raw accuracy retention.
weaknesses: The theory (Sec. 4) is developed entirely for linear/bilinear factorization of a single matrix; its extension to deep nonlinear multi-layer networks is only heuristically motivated and validated empirically (small MNIST 4-layer network), leaving a meaningful gap between the proven guarantees and the actual regime (LLMs/ViTs) where the method is deployed.

For ACIP, the ablated variant without LoRA (i.e., essentially PTS-style selection) performs nearly as well as or better than the full ACIP with adapters, and is not drastically worse than FLEXRANK in some regimes (Fig. 4), which somewhat tempers the magnitude of FLEXRANK's advantage over the strongest existing baseline.

Training costs are non-trivial: the paper acknowledges roughly 2x memory overhead and 2x slower training than a dense forward pass due to teacher-student distillation and un-fused factorized layers, which is presented as an implementation limitation but is not addressed with actual optimized implementation results.

No comparison (even partial or on a small scale) is provided against architecturally elastic methods such as FLEXTRON/LLAMAFLEX or the concurrent nested-subspace work (Rauba & van der Schaar, 2026), despite both being discussed at length in the appendix/related work; the stated reasons (no public code, proprietary data) are understandable but leave the comparative positioning against the closest competing paradigm untested.

For the DINOv3/ImageNet experiments, only the classification head is finetuned while the backbone remains frozen at pretrained weights before decomposition; this simplifies the setting relative to the LLM experiments and may inflate the apparent robustness of FLEXRANK, since much of the network's representational capacity is not being actively adapted during elastic training.

Fig. 4 and Fig. 5 results (the main comparative results) are reported without confidence intervals, error bars, or multiple seeds, unlike Table 1, making it harder to assess the statistical significance of the reported gaps between FLEXRANK and baselines, particularly at extreme compression ratios where curves appear close.

The validation of the additive-error/ranking-preservation assumption underlying the DP procedure (App. C.3) is conducted on a small MNIST-scale network (4 layers, K=10), and it is unclear how well this generalizes to the much deeper, highly nonlinear Transformer architectures used in the main experiments, where the assumption is most heavily relied upon.

strengths: The paper provides genuine theoretical grounding (Sec. 4, with full proofs in App. B) explaining why post-training selection (PTS) and all-subspace learning (ASL) provably fail to recover Pareto-optimal submodels, and why nested subspace learning (NSL) succeeds in the linear-model setting. This is a clear conceptual contribution beyond the usual heuristic justifications common in the elastic-model literature.

Empirical evaluation spans multiple architectures and scales (GPT-2, Llama-3.2-1B/3B, Llama-3.1-8B, DINOv3 ViT-L to ViT-7B), with consistent improvements over closely related baselines (SVD, DataSVD, ACIP with/without LoRA) in accuracy-vs-parameter trade-off curves (Fig. 4).

The Gauge-Aligned Reparametrization (GAR) is a practical and non-trivial contribution that converts rank savings into actual measured inference speedups (Fig. 10), and is applied uniformly to all rank-based baselines for a fair comparison.

Extensive ablations isolate individual design choices (DataSVD sample efficiency, need for end-to-end vs. per-layer training, importance of nested submodel sampling vs. single-budget training), which substantiate the core claims with more than just aggregate accuracy numbers.

The authors explicitly test the key approximating assumption behind the DP-based rank search (additive-error ranking preservation) in App. C.3, reporting quantitative agreement/violation metrics rather than simply asserting the assumption holds.
weaknesses: The central theoretical results (Thms 4.1-4.3) are proven only for linear two-factor models; their relevance to the deep nonlinear Transformer/ViT settings used in the main experiments is only indirectly supported, since the ranking-preservation assumption underlying the DP submodel search is validated exclusively on a small toy MNIST setup (4 layers, K=10, 10,000 submodels) rather than on the LLMs/ViTs actually evaluated. This leaves a meaningful theory-practice gap.

The paper does not experimentally compare against Rauba & van der Schaar (2026), which is explicitly identified as the closest concurrent work on rank-based elasticity; the comparison is limited to a qualitative paragraph, leaving the marginal contribution of FlexRank's decomposition/GAR components unverified against the nearest competitor.

Training efficiency remains a real practical cost: the paper acknowledges roughly 2x memory overhead and 2x slower high-rank training due to un-fused factorized layers and dual teacher/student forward passes, without resolving this in the reported experiments.

Some explanations for strong results are somewhat speculative post-hoc rationalizations (e.g., attributing the very strong ViT results partly to "ImageNet1K being substantially smaller... allowing more epochs" rather than a controlled ablation isolating this factor).

Baseline comparisons against non-rank-based compression families (pruning, depth-elastic methods, quantization) are limited to a single model (Llama-3.2-1B) and a single figure (Fig. 5), which is thin support for the claim of general competitiveness beyond low-rank approaches.

Variance/robustness reporting is inconsistent: Table 1 reports confidence intervals, but the main Pareto-front comparisons (Figs. 4-5) do not indicate seeds or variance, making it hard to assess whether observed gaps at intermediate budgets are statistically meaningful.

The Impact Statement is essentially a boilerplate non-statement, providing no substantive discussion of potential misuse or deployment risks associated with easily compressible/redistributable elastic models.

strengths: Rigorous theoretical treatment for the linear-model case (Sec. 4, proofs in App. B) rigorously proving why post-training selection (PTS) and all-subspace learning (ASL) provably fail to recover Pareto-optimal submodels, while nested submodel learning (NSL) provably does — this gives a principled justification for the paper's design choices rather than relying purely on heuristics.

Careful empirical validation of the theory in a fully exhaustive, tractable synthetic setting (Fig. 2, Fig. 3) before scaling to real networks, which builds confidence that the qualitative theoretical predictions (PTS/ASL failure, NSL success) transfer to practice.

The key tractability assumption underlying the DP-based global rank search (additive error across layers) is not just asserted but explicitly stress-tested in App. C.3 with quantitative agreement metrics (Spearman ρ=0.991, DP exact-match rate 94.1%, bounded regret), which is a good-faith effort at validating a load-bearing assumption.

Broad and relevant experimental coverage: GPT-2, three Llama model sizes (1B/3B/8B), and DINOv3 ViTs from 300M to 7B parameters, evaluated on both LM zero-shot commonsense tasks and ImageNet1K classification, with comparisons at matched training budgets against a strong and appropriately chosen set of baselines (ACIP as current SOTA, plus SVD/DataSVD, LLM-Pruner, LayerSkip).

The Gauge-Aligned Reparametrization (GAR) is a clean, generally applicable trick with a clear theoretical FLOP reduction and empirical validation (Fig. 10) that closes the gap between naive low-rank factorization and dense compute, and is fairly applied to all rank-based baselines for a fair comparison.

Thorough ablations isolating the individual contributions of the method (initialization sample size, need for end-to-end vs. per-layer distillation, need for joint/nested vs. independent submodel training, layer-wise importance heatmaps), which help attribute gains to specific design choices rather than the method as a whole.
weaknesses: The central theoretical guarantees (Thms 4.1–4.3) are proven only for linear two-factor models; extending this to deep nonlinear Transformers/CNNs relies on the additive-error/layer-independence assumption, which, while empirically probed on a small MNIST-scale setting (App. C.3), is not validated at the scale of the main LLM/ViT experiments, leaving a real theory-practice gap that is somewhat understated in the main text.

A directly relevant concurrent work (Rauba & van der Schaar, 2026) studying rank-based elasticity is discussed only qualitatively (App. A.1) and not compared experimentally, making it hard to assess how much of the reported improvement is attributable to genuinely novel contributions versus concepts already explored concurrently.

Practical utility at aggressive compression appears limited in the post-adaptation setting: Table 1 shows code-domain accuracy collapsing to near-zero (e.g., 1.22% for Llama-3.2-1B at 0.4x) at smaller elastic sizes, which tempers claims of "graceful" degradation for some domains/tasks.

The training-efficiency argument (comparing FlexRank's 5B-token consolidation budget to the 9T-token full pretraining of Llama-3.2-1B) is a somewhat unfair comparison, since the more informative baseline would be the token/compute budget used by competing elastic/compression methods (e.g., ACIP, LayerSkip) rather than full pretraining from scratch; this framing could overstate the efficiency advantage.

GAR's benefits are demonstrated under a compute-bound regime (large matrices/sequences, batch inference); it's unclear how much benefit is retained in more memory-bound LLM decoding regimes (small batch, autoregressive generation) that are common in practical deployment, which is acknowledged only briefly.

Some experimental details (e.g., variance/error bars for the main Fig. 4 results, exact evaluation protocol nuances) are relatively terse in the main text and require appendix cross-referencing, slightly reducing at-a-glance interpretability of the significance of reported gains.

The code availability footnote is left empty in the manuscript, so reproducibility cannot be independently verified from the provided document alone (though this may be an artifact of anonymization/formatting).
